list.listitem: Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade multifocal vascular tumor; typical skin lesions are multifocal, asymmetrically distributed, and nonpruritic.C
For a patient newly diagnosed with KS, exclude underlying human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (acquired immune deficiency syndrome [AIDS]-defining illness).A
Local therapy can be used to treat bulky KS disease and for cosmetic reasons.B
Systemic chemotherapy is indicated for widespread, rapidly progressive, and symptomatic KS.A
Classic KS mainly exhibits an indolent course, whereas endemic, AIDS-associated, and transplant-associated KS tend to behave more aggressively.B

background.definition: Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is a multifocal low-grade vascular tumor.

list.listitem: Classic KS has the highest rates in Mediterranean countries (up to 30 cases per million).
Endemic KS accounts for 10% of all malignant tumors in central Africa. Rates in Africa markedly increased with the AIDS epidemic.

Epidemic (HIV/AIDS-associated) KS occurs 20,000 times more often in patients with advanced HIV who have not had highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) than in the general population. In the post-HAART era (>1996), there has been a noticeable decline in KS.

In the US from 1996‒2018, Kaposi sarcoma was the most common nonkeratinocyte skin cancer (82%) in persons living with HIV, followed by melanoma (12%) and cutaneous lymphoma (2.6%). The incidence rate ratio for persons living with HIV was 149 (95% CI 141 to 153).
Iatrogenic post-transplant KS may occur in up to 0.5% to 5.3% of recipients.

A 2020 cohort study found that viruses, UV radiation exposure, and immunosuppression are associated with the development of nonkeratinocyte skin cancer, including KS, in immunosuppressed solid organ transplant recipients.
KS can affect patients of all ages, but is more common in adults.
KS generally has a predilection for men (15 times greater in men than in women). AIDS-associated KS in Africa has an equal incidence among both genders.
KS is the most common tumor arising in persons living with HIV. For patients with HIV, KS is an AIDS-defining illness.
KS flare (exacerbation) can occur with immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) following initiation of HAART, after corticosteroids, and with rituximab therapy.A
Five epidemiologic forms of KS exist: classic, African endemic, AIDS-associated, iatrogenic, and non-epidemic.
Classic KS mainly affects elderly men (40-70 years) of Mediterranean, Eastern European, or Jewish origin.
African KS is endemic in central Africa, affecting both children and adolescents (5-15 years) and adults (20-40 years).
AIDS-associated KS arises in persons living with HIV, usually (but not exclusively) with low CD4 cell counts.
Iatrogenic KS is associated with immunosuppression from drugs (corticosteroids, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, and cyclosporine) or arises 20 to 30 months after solid-organ transplantation.
Non-epidemic KS includes a rare subset of immunocompetent, HIV-negative individuals, typically males, who have a smiilar presentation as that of classic KS with a good prognosis.
Patients with congenital immunodeficiency are not at increased risk for developing KS.

KS is associated with human herpes virus 8 (HHV8)/KS herpes virus infection. Several viral genes are involved in KS tumorigenesis, including latency-associated nuclear antigen (LANA or LNA-1), viral cyclin, v-FLIP.
KS is an angioproliferative lesion of lymphatic vessel origin. KS tumors can be clonal. However, they are believed to represent multifocal reactive proliferations rather than true malignancies.
KS lesions are composed of spindled shaped tumor cells, abnormal vessels, and admixed chronic inflammatory cells.
Lesions evolve through 3 stages: early patch, to plaque, and later to tumor nodules. All epidemiologic subtypes have similar histopathology.
HIV coinfection is synergistic, resulting in more aggressive and widespread KS disease.
KS regression can occur spontaneously (rare), following appropriate therapy, or after removal of immunosuppressive therapy.

list.listitem: Careful dermatological examination (including the oral mucosa) is indicated for patients at risk for KS, including elderly men of Mediterranean or Jewish origin, those with HIV infection, those on immunosuppressive therapy, and transplant recipients.A
In persons living wth HIV, antiretroviral therapy without treatment interruptions may prevent KS or result in a less aggressive presentation.A
Screen transplant recipients and donors for HHV8 infection.B
KS is a low-grade multifocal vascular tumor; typical skin lesions are multifocal, asymmetrically distributed, and nonpruritic. Their size and color varies from pink, red, purple, and brown to blue.C
Exclude underlying HIV infection or immunosuppression in a patient presenting with KS.A
Tissue biopsy is required to distinguish KS from its mimics.B

Differential.Differential_Features: Vascular lesions typically involve skin, but may affect lypmh nodes, the respiratory tract, and bone. Associated with Bartonella infection. Biopsy shows capillaries with neutrophils.
Mucocutaneous location. Biopsy shows a lobular capillary hemangioma pattern.
Benign vascular skin lesion. Biopsy shows vascular lobules.
Associated with chronic venous stasis or arteriovenous anomalies. Biopsy shows vascular hyperplasia of preexisting vessels.
Petechiae or purpura commonly on the lower extremities. Biopsy shows perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes, red blood cell extravasation, and hemosiderin deposition. Closely resembles regressed KS.
Infiltrating vascular tumor, purpuric in apperance with occasional telangiectasias, mostly involving the extremities. LNA-1 negative on biopsy.
Vascular neoplasm with cytologic atypia. Frequently LNA-1 negative.

list.listitem: Patients with KS may be asymptomatic. Typical skin lesions are multifocal, asymmetrically distributed, and nonpruritic. Cutaneous KS mostly occur on the lower extremities, face, oral mucosa, and genitalia. KS of the foot may cause pain with ambulation. Lesion size and color vary, ranging from pink, red, purple, brown to blue. Cutaneous KS may be more difficult to distinguish in dark-skinned people. Lesions may appear papular, plaque-like, bullous-like, or fungating. Skin ulceration and secondary infection can occur. Long-standing lesions may become indurated (woody) and develop a verrucous or hyperkeratotic appearance. KS can mimic dermatofibromas, other vascular entities, melanocytic lesions, hematomas, cutaneous lymphoma, or gouty tophi.
Lymphedema of the legs, genitalia, and face may be painful, out of proportion to the extent of KS disease, and can mask underlying KS.
Intraoral lesions may cause pain, bleeding, and ulceration, and may affect mastication, speech, and swallowing. KS involves mainly the palate, followed by the gingiva, and less often the tongue.
Conjunctival KS can cause red or bloody eyes, a mucopurulent discharge, or visual disturbance. Ecchymotic KS variant may manifest with periorbital ecchymoses.
Primary visceral KS without mucocutaneous involvement is uncommon.

Gastrointestinal (GI) tract KS may be asymptomatic or can cause weight loss, abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, ileus, upper or lower GI bleeding, malabsorption, intestinal obstruction, or diarrhea.
KS of the respiratory system can present with shortness of breath, fever, cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, and serosanguineous effusions.
Psychosocial stress can accompany the appearance of KS (related to HIV stigma, cosmesis, ostracism, and loss of employment).
The following tests should be part of the initial evaluation: HIV testing, chest x-ray, fecal occult blood test, and confirmatory tissue biopsy.
HIV test: 4th genderation (includes HIV antibody and p24 antigen detection) screening test for HIV infection (if positive, a CD4 cell count and HIV viral load).

Chest x-ray: to evaluate for pulmonary KS. Chest x-ray may show nodular opacities, interstitial and/or alveolar infiltrates, interlobular septal thickening with peribronchovascular predominance, pleural effusion, or hilar and/or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Solitary nodule formation is rare. CT scan is slightly better than radiography for identifying thoracic KS. Concomitant pulmonary infection must be excluded.
Fecal occult blood test: to screen for GI tract KS.

Confirmatory tissue biopsy: to demonstrate a vascular lesion that contains HHV8 (LNA-1-immunopositive staining) and expresses vascular (CD31, CD34) and lymphatic (D2-40) markers. Pathological histology is similar among various subtypes (patch, plaque, and nodular stages) and typically inlcudes spindle-shaped cells, leukocytic infiltration and neoangiogenesis. Bleeding after biopsy is rare, except in the pulmonary system. Early patch stage is subtle on biopsy and may go unnoticed by the unwary.
The following tests should be guided by symptoms: bronchoscopy, GI endoscopy, and imaging of tissue and bone.
Bronchoscopy: to identify lesions in the tracheobronchial tree.
GI endoscopy: to identify isolated or confluent KS lesions. The submucosal nature of KS lesions makes them difficult to biopsy.
CT scans and MRI: for evaluating deep nodal KS and involvement of deep tissue planes. Bone lesions are better detected by CT scan and MRI; they frequently go undetected on plain x-ray or bone scans.
For patients requiring systemic chemotherapy, evaluate for renal, hepatic, and bone marrow function as well as overall performance status.
Determine the extent of KS mucocutaneous lesions, evaluate for the presence of lymphadenopathy, and obtain an HIV test.
Screen for GI tract KS by testing for fecal occult blood.
Imaging studies (chest x-ray) can be used to evaluate for KS of the respiratory system.
Biopsy a suspected KS lesion for a confirmatory diagnosis, except for laryngeal and pulmonary KS lesions (which may cause significant bleeding, with emergent respiratory compromise).
Treatment goals include symptom palliation; prevention of KS progression; improvement of cosmesis; and abatement of associated edema, organ compromise, and psychological stress.C
Topical treatments for localized cutaneous KS include topical alitretinoin, imiquimod and timolol.

Indications for systemic chemotherapy include widespread skin involvement (>25 lesions), extensive oral KS, marked symptomatic edema, rapidly progressive disease, symptomatic visceral KS, and KS flare.A

Optimal control of HIV infection using antiretroviral therapy is a key component in the treatment of AIDS-associated KS, and antiretroviral therapy alone may be sufficient for regression of mild to moderate cutaneous KS.A
Liposomal anthracyclines (doxorubicin or daunorubicin) are used as first-line systemic treatments for KS.A
Taxanes have efficacy as second-line systemic treatment for KS.A

A 2020 trial evaluating alternative chemotherapy options in resource limited settings randomized 334 patients with AIDS associated KS in Africa. All patients received anti-retroviral therapy and were randomised to bleomycin/vincristine, oral etoposide or the control arm of paclitaxel. The trial was stopped early due to inferior progression free survival in the experimental arms, with the conclusion that paclitaxel remains the most effective option in this setting.
KS may be associated with upregulation of mTOR, PDGF, VEGF and ckit, which suggests that targeted inhibitors may offer therapeutic potential.C
Treatment options are similar for the different epidemiologic forms of KS.A

Patients with AIDS-associated KS should receive HAART, which may be the only treatment needed for KS regression in those with limited cutaneous KS lesions. KS flare alone following HAART should not be considered treatment failure or warrant antiretroviral regimen change.
For first-line therapy use either (1) pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (Doxil or Caelyx) 20 mg/square meter every 3 weeks or (2) liposomal daunorubicin (DaunoXome) 40 mg/square meter every 2 weeks.

For second-line therapy use paclitaxel 100 mg/square meter every 2 to 3 weeks. Reduced steroid premedication should be used. Careful observation for toxicity related to possible antiretroviral drug interaction is necessary in HIV-positive patients.
Vinorelbine may be effective for AIDS-related KS in patients who have failed other therapies.
Novel therapies include interferon-α, thalidomide, COL-3, antiherpes therapy, imatinib (Gleevec), and glycyrrhizic acid. Topical alitretinoin is effective for cutaneous KS.
An early 2019 report with just 6 patients reported a 100% response treating cutaneous KS type lesions with twice daily topical tacrolimus for a year.

A small randomized trial compared imiquimod with cryotherapy in 50 lesions in 8 patients with classic Kaposi sarcoma. Outcomes were similar between the groups. Imiquimod 5% was applied three times a week for 12 weeks versus cryotherapy every 3 weeks.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of immune checkpoint PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, such as pembrolizumab, nivolumab, atezolizumab, durvalumab, and avelumab, found a pooled objective response rate (ORR) of 61%, with 17% achieving complete response, and the disease control rate (DCR) was 91% for patients with Kaposi's sarcoma.
Cryotherapy can be used for local therapy.
Surgical excision should be restricted for cosmetically disturbing lesions, to alleviate discomfort, or to control local tumor growth such as conjunctival KS obscuring vision.

Local therapy to manage bulky lesions or for cosmesis includes external beam radiation (8-12 Gy), laser therapy, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, topical Panretin gel (alitretinoin 0.1%), or intralesional vinblastine (0.2-0.3 mg/mL solution with a volume of 0.1 mL per 0.5 square centimeters of lesion).
For iatrogenic KS, consider adjusting immunosuppressive therapy. The introduction of sirolimus (rapamycin) should be considered for patients with posttransplant KS.B
Radiation sequelae for KS include skin damage, hypopigmentation, hyperpigmentation, fibrosis, lymphedema, and severe mucositis.

A systematic review of electrochemotherapy using electroporation and IV bleomycin in 1-6 treatment sessions of KS skin lesions revealed a complete response rate of 65-100% with mild and transient toxicity, and may be a promising treatment option that requires further long-term disease control analysis and comparison to other therapies.
Classic KS has an indolent course. The median survival is years to decades. Rapid disease with visceral involvement is infrequent.A
African KS follows a more aggressive course. The median survival is months to years. The lymphadenopathic form has a poor prognosis.A
AIDS-associated KS without antiretroviral therapy is a progressive disease with a median survival of months to possibly years.A
Transplant-associated KS has a protracted but aggressive course. Median survival is months to years.A
In general, factors that portend a poor prognosis include visceral and pulmonary involvement and concomitant HIV-related illness.A
Reports of KS in pregnancy are rare. Pregnant women often present with advanced disease and delayed diagnosis because KS is not suspected.
African (endemic) KS in children presents with gross lymphadenopathy and a fulminant course.
Childhood AIDS-associated KS occurs mainly in sub-Saharan Africa, probably related to high HHV8 infection rates.
